NB I’ve developed this map more practically in the rest of the method, which is why I’m comfortable publishing this provisional synthesis (parts of which are directly research based, the whole of which is my own):

i) child on her own – orientation and external safety

ii) child with borrowed adult – experience of at least one good adult function, personified by a real/remembered/imagined/symbolic figure

iii) adult as apprentice – with help, adult tries to do at least one part of looking after the child

iv) adult in her own right – adult repeats as many times as necessary, to build up the capacity to summon it at will: offering the child warmth, protection and direction

v) adult in relation to child – adult in charge but not banishing child, child no longer solely responsible for managing life

The child doesn’t need to stop being a child – you just become bigger than the child-state. A useful saying to yourself might be: ‘I don’t need to stop being this child, but I am also becoming an adult…’

Sometimes we may notice when we’ve been hooked, before we know what part of us has been hooked. Sometimes it may be a bit later, perhaps after we’ve noticed the tightening in our jaw or the getting involved of our stomach and the writing of half of the text message we really, really shouldn’t be sending. In which case it may be a good idea to forget about finding out who’s hooked for the moment – Child, Protector, past hurt. Our hand may already be reaching for a glass of wine or turning to our phones or forming an opinion about our relationship. Pema Chodron has a great word for this tightening/urge – shenpa.

So, let’s just notice that we’ve been hooked. If we can take a breath or two (or three) and finish what we were doing (assuming no-one is in danger) all the better. If we don’t manage to take the breaths to settle down, we may at least have time to summon enough Adult to be nice to the Child, or Protector to stop us doing something stupid, or simply say to ourselves ‘not yet’.

response.text: Sometimes you'll notice you're hooked before you know which part of you is doing the hooking. Sometimes you won't notice it until you've already tensed up your jaw, or whatever, and until you've already done some part of reacting—until you've already written half the text, for example. It's okay to forget, for the time being, to try to figure out which part it is. Just be aware, as Pema Chödron has explained , that there's a kind of tightening, a kind of "I need to do something" sensation that comes before you finish making up the story. She calls this shenpa .

response.text:
Monogamy, particularly the sexual aspect of it, has become much more important since agriculture, and the advent of property and inheritance. By the Industrial Revolution it was being universally enforced in some strict form, often through both law and social pressure. Prior to that, there were many tribal cultures that were far more relaxed about allowing sexual and even emotional contact with others outside of the primary partnership. I believe the term "social monogamy" has been coined to describe this.

I took this idea to its logical extreme. I told B, when she told me she wanted to marry me, that although I wanted to marry her, I was still sexually attracted to other women. Thus I felt that it would not be right for me to marry her until I could fix that. My actual words to her were, "It's not fair of me to commit to you while I am still sexually attracted to other women, so it's necessary for me to work on that before we get married."
